snippets: DPR usually refers to the finetuning process too, not just the inference steps of encode the text and vector search. As for OP question about why DPR seems to be out of popularity, I think it is just that fine tuning in general is more difficult and time-consuming to get a result immediately so people just like to use pretrained model directly.

Moreover, in RAG pipeline I think there are a lot of ways to achieve a better result such as better data cleaning, chunking etc.. finetuning method like DPR is usually the last step to do to improve the performance. Here are some points I would like to note: DPR is a fine tuning method, so like you said people must have compute resources and not everybody have it. DPR requires training data with labels i.e question-passage pairs, and constructing the dataset can time consuming and costly. Compared that to directly using a pretrained model that are trained on billions of data by big companies, it is a much more complicated process.

And in most cases, a single encoder is good enough. I think DPR idea is still used a lot even nowadays. If you read the blog/paper of some of the most popular embeddings like Cohere or OpenAI, you would find that their method is the same as DPR, they just use a single model instead of 2 and train on much more data. There are also some variants of DPR, e.g. finetune an adapter on top of the pretrained model as question encoder and freeze the weight for passage encoder, that way you do not have to reindex the database every time you retrain the model.

I'm also curious why does your company use DPR, and what base model(s) are you finetuning your embeddings from? ... First I think you should have an evaluation metrics to judge how good the model is, usually recall is used as metrics. Then you should try some of the available pretrained model to see if it is good enough for your use case. If it is not good then you can try fine tune the model. In the fine tuning phase you can try using 2 encoders or single encoder, then you compare the 2 approaches to see which is better.

At run-time, DPR applies a different encoder EQ(.) that maps the input question to a d-dimensional vector, and retrieves k passages of which vectors are the closest to the question vector. The similarity between the question and the passage is using the dot product:

However, with the advent of pre-trained language models (PLMs) such as BERT (Devlin, 2018), representing passages or queries as dense vectors has gradually become the mainstream approach.
